text:
# Anti-Aliasing and Filtering

Also called: Box filter, Gaussian filter, Volume Filter

## Overview
Anti-Aliasing and Filtering in volume rendering addresses the visual artifacts caused by undersampling, including jagged edges, flickering, and high-frequency noise, by smoothing the transition between discrete samples and continuous geometry. This family encompasses methods that operate at different stages of the pipeline: pre-filtering data to prevent discretization errors, spatial filtering during rasterization (such as [splatting](#23-splatting.md)), and post-processing screen-space blurs. It is distinct from sibling methods like [Interpolation and Sampling Techniques](2787-interpolation-and-sampling-techniques.md) because it focuses on the suppression of high-frequency components in the final image or intermediate buffers rather than the accuracy of individual sample retrieval.

## Shared principles
The family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating the rendered image or volumetric data as a discrete function that requires smoothing to approximate the continuous signal [S1].

1.  **Image Representation**: The input is an image $L$, defined as a discrete two-dimensional function $L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$. For each pixel position $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{N}^2$, the function returns the color $L(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ [S1].
2.  **Color Space and Range**: The color channels (red, green, blue) are assumed to be non-negative real numbers. For High Dynamic Range (HDR) images, the values can range from $0$ to $+\infty$ [S1].
3.  **Screen-Space Constraint**: Many techniques in this family operate exclusively on information currently visible on the screen. They cannot access data for objects behind the camera or occluded geometry that was not rendered in the base pass [S1].
4.  **Convolution Basis**: Many techniques apply a filter to the original image or splat footprint, typically using neighborhood-based convolution. The new color or contribution of a pixel is determined by its neighbors [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells](829-splatting-for-anti-aliasing-small-cells.md)
This method prevents the loss of geometric detail in adaptive meshes by rendering small volumetric cells as [anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats](#829-splatting-for-anti-aliasing-small-cells.md) instead of polygons, addressing the problem where small cells are missed between slice planes or by pixel samples during [scan conversion](#8321-nearest-neighbor-ray-traversal.md). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by replacing complex filtered polygon rendering with hardware-accelerated texture-mapped Gaussian splats, ensuring that high-gradient regions in unstructured grids contribute to the image without the bandwidth overhead of small polygons.

### [Motion-Blurred Splats](1343-motion-blurred-splats.md)
[Motion-Blurred Splats](#1343-motion-blurred-splats.md) extends standard splatting to handle temporal aliasing by approximating the integration of voxel energy over a shutter interval. It solves the flickering and scintillation artifacts caused by rapid movement or spinning in volume rendering by smoothing temporal variations, though it does not address visibility changes or popping artifacts caused by sorting order changes. Unlike standard splatting, which suffers from aliasing during rapid motion, this method integrates energy over time by stretching the spatial footprint of each splat along its projected motion vector.

### [Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing](1447-threshold-slicing-and-anti-aliasing.md)
[Threshold Slicing and Anti-Aliasing](#1447-threshold-slicing-and-anti-aliasing.md) is a hybrid volume rendering technique that partitions volumetric data based on a scalar value threshold to optimize rendering quality and performance. It addresses the problem of aliasing artifacts and geometric inaccuracies that arise when rendering unstructured or curvilinear grids using standard rasterization methods. Unlike pure splatting, which may blur sharp features, or pure polygonal slicing, which struggles with complex topologies and gaps, this method renders high-value cells as precise polygons and low-value cells as anti-aliased ellipsoidal splats.

### [Prefiltering](2928-prefiltering.md)
[Prefiltering](#2928-prefiltering.md) is a technique used in volume rendering to remove singularity-like artifacts and avoid discretization errors, particularly in participating media with insufficient optical thickness to naturally blur sampled illumination. It differs from naive prefiltering of source illumination by being adaptive, allowing the perception of background illumination features while smoothing out high-frequency noise.

### [PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter](8374-pseudoseparable-cross-bilateral-filter.md)
The [PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter](#8374-pseudoseparable-cross-bilateral-filter.md) is a two-pass screen-space filtering technique used to [smooth ambient occlusion](#10956-smooth-vertex-lighting-with-ambient-occlusion-effect.md) (AO) data while preserving geometric edges defined by depth discontinuities and surface normals. It solves the problem of AO bleeding across object boundaries or sharp creases by using a bilateral weighting scheme that considers the similarity of neighboring pixels' depth and normal values. It is distinguished from standard Gaussian blurs by its edge-preserving nature and from full 2D [bilateral filters](#8983-bilateral-filter.md) by its separable implementation, which reduces computational cost at the expense of some cross-axis coherence.

### [Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing](8804-separable-ping-pong-blur-post-processing.md)
This method applies a separable Gaussian blur to a rendered scene to reduce aliasing artifacts and smooth the final image. It solves the problem of high-frequency noise and jagged edges in splatted volume renderings by decoupling the 2D convolution into two 1D passes. It differs from [Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells](829-splatting-for-anti-aliasing-small-cells.md) by applying filtering in post-processing rather than during primitive rasterization, and from [Prefiltering](2928-prefiltering.md) by operating on the final color buffer rather than precomputing mipmaps.

### [Screen-Space Image Filtering](9037-screen-space-image-filtering.md)
[Screen-Space Image Filtering](#9037-screen-space-image-filtering.md) modifies a pre-rendered "vacuum" image by applying [neighborhood-based filters](#4472-donerf-depth-oracle-filtering.md) to simulate effects caused by participating media, using only the pixel data currently available on the screen. Unlike volumetric methods that reconstruct geometry or ray-cast through volume data, this family operates on the final 2D image buffer, treating it as a discrete function to be convolved or adjusted. It is distinct from its siblings because it does not rely on splatting primitives, pre-filtered textures, or specific anti-aliasing kernels during the geometry pass, but rather applies post-processing or screen-space operations to the accumulated color buffer.

### Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing
**Definition**: Calculates an anti-aliasing factor based on the distance of a point from a line, scaled by viewport and FOV [S2, unofficial]. The factor represents the pixel size relative to the distance; smaller pixel-projected distance results in smaller AA [S2, unofficial].
**Step**: Return `distance / uViewportSize.y * uFovY` [S2, unofficial].
**Parameter**: `uFovY` is the vertical field of view, and `uViewportSize` is the viewport dimensions in pixels (width, height) [S2, unofficial].

### Screen Space Ratio (SSR) with Perspective Filter
**Definition**: Calculates the Screen Space Ratio (SSR) for a texture coordinate to determine sampling density or filtering strength, optionally applying a perspective filter to soften the result [S3, unofficial]. It calculates the SSR based on projection matrix, position, object scale, and screen dimensions, used for font scaling [S3, unofficial].
**Step**: If Filter is true: compute derivatives $a = \text{float2}(\text{ddx}(UV.x), \text{ddy}(UV.x))$ and $b = \text{float2}(\text{ddx}(UV.y), \text{ddy}(UV.y))$; compute $s = \text{lerp}(\text{dot}(a,a), \text{dot}(b,b), 0.5)$; set $\text{SSR} = \text{rsqrt}(s) / \text{TextureSize}$ [S3, unofficial]. If Filter is false: compute $s = \text{rsqrt}(|\text{ddx}(UV.x) \cdot \text{ddy}(UV.y) - \text{ddy}(UV.x) \cdot \text{ddx}(UV.y)|)$; set $\text{SSR} = s / \text{TextureSize}$ [S3, unofficial]. Set $\text{pixelSize} = \text{position}.w$; divide $\text{pixelSize}$ by $(\text{objectScale} \cdot \text{mul}((\text{float2x2})\text{projection}, \text{float2}(\text{screenWidth}, \text{screenHeight})))$; compute $\text{SSR} = \text{rsqrt}(\text{dot}(\text{pixelSize}, \text{pixelSize}) \cdot 2) \cdot \text{fontScale}$ [S3, unofficial].

### Center-Precomputed MIP Filter
**Definition**: An anti-aliasing technique that precomputes MIP-filtered parameters at the surfel center during preprocessing to reduce per-pixel rasterization cost while eliminating aliasing artifacts [S4, unofficial].
**Step**: Store the resulting MIP-filtered inverse covariance $\Sigma^{-1}_{\text{mip}}$ and normalization factor $\alpha_{\text{norm}}$ once per primitive [S4, unofficial]. During rasterization, load these four parameters from shared memory [S4, unofficial]. Apply the parameters directly to the intersection coordinates via the quadratic form of equation 6 [S4, unofficial].
**Number**: Rendering time is 50 ms per frame for the center-precomputed MIP filter, an overhead of only 8 ms (<20%) over the unfiltered baseline of 42 ms [S4, unofficial].
**Comparison**: Compared to per-pixel Jacobian evaluation (AA-2DGS), this method is visually indistinguishable but faster (50 ms vs 65 ms per frame) because it avoids computing the full 2x2 Jacobian, its outer product, and matrix inverse at every covered pixel [S4, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of filtering in volume rendering has evolved alongside hardware capabilities. Early methods relied on simple box filters for crisp edges in high-resolution volumes, while Gaussian filters were introduced to prevent banding artifacts [S1]. The introduction of splatting techniques, such as those by Zwicker et al., allowed for efficient anti-aliasing of unstructured grids by projecting 3D kernels into 2D ellipsoids [S1, citing [5]]. More recent developments include adaptive prefiltering for participating media to handle singularity artifacts [S1] and screen-space bilateral filters for preserving edges in post-processing [S1].
